items.followUp: State two differences between distance and displacement, giving one example of each.

rubric.why: Distinguishes scalar and vector quantities by direction.
rubric.description: Defines scalars as having magnitude only and vectors as having both magnitude and direction.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for correctly stating the distinction.

rubric.why: Examples show the student can identify scalar and vector quantities.
rubric.description: Gives suitable examples of a scalar and a vector.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for one correct example of each.

modelAnswer: A scalar quantity has magnitude only, whereas a vector quantity has both magnitude and direction.
Mass and time are scalars; force and velocity are vectors.

items.followUp: Define a scalar quantity and give two examples.

rubric.why: Kinematics describes motion without explaining what causes it.
rubric.description: Defines kinematics as the study or description of motion without considering its causes.
rubric.how: Award 2 marks for the complete definition; 1 mark if motion is mentioned but the distinction from causes is missing.

modelAnswer: Kinematics is the branch of physics that describes the motion of objects without considering the causes of that motion.

items.followUp: Define stress and state its SI unit.

rubric.why: Young’s modulus is defined by the ratio of tensile stress to tensile strain within the elastic limit.
rubric.description: States the definition of Young’s modulus.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the correct stress-to-strain ratio and elastic-limit condition.

rubric.why: The SI unit of Young’s modulus is the pascal, equivalent to newtons per square metre.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for Pa or N/m².

modelAnswer: Young’s modulus is the ratio of tensile stress to tensile strain, provided the material is within its elastic limit.
Its SI unit is the pascal (Pa), equivalent to N/m².

items.followUp: What instrument is used to measure the relative density of a liquid?

rubric.why: A suitable hydrometer, specifically a lactometer for milk, can be used for this measurement.
rubric.description: States that milk density can be measured with a suitable hydrometer or lactometer.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for a clear yes and a suitable instrument.

rubric.why: A hydrometer’s level of immersion depends on the liquid’s density; a lactometer is calibrated for milk.
rubric.description: Explains the instrument’s use or identifies the milk-specific hydrometer.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for linking immersion to density or identifying the lactometer as the milk instrument.

modelAnswer: Yes. A suitable hydrometer can be used; the special hydrometer used for milk is called a lactometer.
Its depth of immersion depends on the density of the liquid.

items.followUp: State the parallelogram rule for finding the resultant of two forces.

rubric.why: The rule requires placing the tail of each successive vector at the head of the preceding one.
rubric.description: Describes how the vectors are arranged head to tail.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the correct arrangement.

rubric.why: The resultant is the vector joining the initial point to the final point of the chain.
rubric.description: States how to draw the resultant.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for giving its correct direction from the first tail to the last head.

modelAnswer: Draw the force vectors to scale, placing the tail of each new vector at the head of the previous one.
The resultant is drawn from the tail of the first vector to the head of the last vector, with its direction shown.

items.followUp: State the first condition for equilibrium of a body.

rubric.why: Rotational equilibrium requires the algebraic sum of torques about any point to be zero.
rubric.description: States the second condition for equilibrium using net torque or balanced moments.
rubric.how: Award 2 marks for stating that net torque is zero or clockwise and anticlockwise moments balance; award 1 mark if torque is mentioned but the condition is incomplete.

modelAnswer: The second condition for equilibrium is that the net torque on the body about any point is zero.
Thus, the sum of clockwise torques equals the sum of anticlockwise torques.

items.followUp: Why is an ideal machine not completely achievable in practice?

rubric.why: Real systems experience resistive forces, especially friction and air resistance.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for naming friction, air resistance, or another relevant resistive force.

rubric.why: Resistive forces dissipate energy, so a real system cannot be perfectly ideal.
rubric.description: Explains the consequence of resistive forces or states that a perfectly ideal system is unattainable.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for linking resistance to energy loss or lack of perfect efficiency.

modelAnswer: An ideal system cannot be achieved in daily life because real systems experience friction and other resistive forces.
These forces dissipate energy, often as heat or sound, so the system cannot be perfectly efficient.

items.followUp: Why is solar energy called a renewable form of energy?

rubric.why: Fossil fuels take geological timescales to form.
rubric.description: States that fossil fuels form very slowly, over millions of years.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the long formation time.

rubric.why: They are consumed much faster than nature can replace them, so their supply is finite on human timescales.
rubric.description: Explains that fossil fuels are not replenished quickly enough to replace what is used.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that consumption exceeds replenishment or that reserves are finite.

modelAnswer: Fossil fuels take millions of years to form.
They are used much faster than nature can replace them, so their reserves are finite and they are called non-renewable.
